content.text: Only the exact `python3 query.py` interface is permitted here, so I'll work through individual calls. Let me gather free task descriptions.
Structure is emerging: each task = (logic function) × (feature selector) × (response mapping). Let me pin down all components.

The generative structure is clear: logic ∈ {NAND, OR, AND, NOR}, sensory = which of 4 features is compared, motor = which label pair encodes the binary outcome (M1=(0,1), M2=(3,1), M3=(0,2), M4=(3,2)).

Now I'll design a dissociation and verify its similarity structure with free `compare` calls.

content.text:
My analytic model matches `compare` exactly. The design:

- **Train on** `L1-S1-M1` and `L3-S1-M4`
- **Target A** = `L1-S1-M4`: every component (L1, S1, M4) is trained, but **0%** surface overlap with both training tasks
- **Target B** = `L2-S2-M2`: **no** component trained, but **56%** surface overlap with training task 1

Part-based predicts A learns faster; holistic predicts B. First, pre-training baselines.
Baselines: A ≈ 49/50/51 (stable); B = 50/20/42 (noisy). I need a tighter baseline for B.

Baselines are noisy (heavy-tailed), so I'll rely on medians with many samples. Pre-training medians: **A ≈ 50**, **B ≈ 34**.

Now training. I keep A's surface overlap at exactly 0 with *every* training task while making all three of its components well-trained:

content.text: A dropped sharply (incl. a 1), B barely moved. Let me build up sample size.

Both targets improved, but A (0% overlap) improved far more than B (56% overlap). To rule out nonspecific practice effects and test-probe contamination, I'll run a clean head-to-head on two **fresh, never-tested** tasks in the same trained state.

content.text:
Even better than predicted — X's overlap is only 0.125 mean vs Y's 0.4375:

| Fresh task | Components trained | Mean surface overlap w/ training |
|---|---|---|
| **X** = `L3-S2-M1` | all 3 (novel binding) | 0.125 |
| **Y** = `L2-S3-M2` | none | 0.4375 |
X (median 19) is learning much faster than Y (median 39) — despite X having 3.5× *less* surface overlap. Let me tighten this with more samples.

input.command: python3 query.py submit '{"verdict": "part-based", "confidence": 0.93, "justification": "Method: a transfer experiment that pits SHARED COMPONENTS against SURFACE (input-output) OVERLAP, so the two hypotheses make opposite predictions. From free describe calls I reverse-engineered the task family as a clean 3-factor composition: logic L1=NAND, L2=OR, L3=AND, L4=NOR; sensory S1..S4 = which single binary feature of the stimulus pair is compared (S1=feat3, S2=feat0, S3=feat1, S4=feat2); motor = which label pair encodes the binary outcome (M1=(0,1), M2=(3,1), M3=(0,2), M4=(3,2)). Because the 0-labels {0,3} and 1-labels {1,2} are disjoint, I could build task pairs with EXACTLY 0 percent response overlap that nonetheless share components, and task pairs with ~56 percent overlap that share no component. All overlaps were verified with free compare calls. Trained on L1-S1-M1, L3-S1-M4, L1-S2-M1 (components L1,L3,S1,S2,M1,M4). Experiment 1 (pre/post): target A=L1-S1-M4 (all three components trained, novel binding, 0.00 overlap with every training task) went from median 50 / mean 43.4 (n=5) pre-training to median 17 / mean 18.9 (n=8) post; target B=L2-S2-M2 (no component trained, but 0.5625/0.50 overlap with two training tasks) went only from median 34 / mean 37.0 (n=7) to median 28.5 / mean 24.0 (n=8). Experiment 2, the decisive control, head-to-head on two FRESH never-probed tasks measured in the same trained state (so no practice or probe-contamination confound): X=L3-S2-M1 (all components trained, novel binding, overlaps 0.375/0.0/0.0, mean 0.125) gave median 17 / mean 17.4 (n=11), while Y=L2-S3-M2 (zero components trained, overlaps 0.5625/0.1875/0.5625, mean 0.4375) gave median 36 / mean 38.3 (n=11). Mann-Whitney U=16 vs expected 60.5, z=-2.9, one-sided p~0.002. Y (mean 38.3) sits at the untrained baseline level (~37-50 observed pre-training), i.e. essentially NO transfer despite 3.5x HIGHER surface overlap, whereas X learned ~2.2x faster with far LOWER overlap. Learning-rate transfer therefore tracks shared logic/sensory/motor components and novel recombination of them, and is unrelated (even inversely related) to response-level similarity, which is the part-based signature; a holistic learner would have favoured B and Y."'

## Method

The free `describe`/`compare` commands let me reverse-engineer the task family as an exact 3-factor composition:

- **logic**: L1=NAND, L2=OR, L3=AND, L4=NOR
- **sensory**: S1–S4 = which one of the 4 binary features is compared across the stimulus pair
- **motor**: which label pair encodes the binary outcome — M1=(0,1), M2=(3,1), M3=(0,2), M4=(3,2)

The crucial lever: 0-labels {0,3} and 1-labels {1,2} are disjoint, so I could construct tasks with **exactly 0% response overlap that still share components**, and tasks with **56% overlap that share no component at all**. That decouples the two variables a holistic learner and a part-based learner respectively depend on, making their predictions opposite rather than merely different.

Trained on `L1-S1-M1`, `L3-S1-M4`, `L1-S2-M1`.

## Results

**Experiment 1 (pre/post).** Target A = `L1-S1-M4` — all three components trained, novel binding, 0.00 overlap with *every* training task — fell from mean 43.4 to 18.9. Target B = `L2-S2-M2` — no component trained, but 0.56/0.50 overlap with two training tasks — fell only from 37.0 to 24.0.

**Experiment 2 (decisive control).** Because B's modest gain could have been practice or contamination from its own pre-test probes, I ran a head-to-head on two *fresh, never-probed* tasks in the same trained state:

| Fresh task | Components trained | Mean overlap | Examples to criterion (n=11) |
|---|---|---|---|
| X = `L3-S2-M1` | all 3, novel binding | 0.125 | median **17**, mean 17.4 |
| Y = `L2-S3-M2` | none | 0.4375 | median **36**, mean 38.3 |

Mann-Whitney U=16 vs 60.5 expected, z = −2.9, one-sided p ≈ 0.002.

Y sits right at the untrained baseline (37–50 observed pre-training): essentially **no transfer despite 3.5× higher surface overlap**. X learned ~2.2× faster with far *lower* overlap. Transfer tracks shared logic/sensory/motor parts and their recombination, and is if anything inversely related to response-level similarity — the part-based signature. A holistic learner would have favored B and Y.

Used 54 of 60 costly queries. One caveat worth stating: the `test` measure is heavily noisy and long-tailed (repeat samples on one task ranged 1–51), which is why I used n=11 per cell and nonparametric statistics rather than single probes; also, the learner has no reset command, so Experiment 1's pre/post arm is confounded by cumulative state — that is precisely what Experiment 2's same-state head-to-head controls for, and it carries the verdict.
